utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis. I am assisted today by our intern, Lisa Hartog, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant, and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to great everyone present today on the 22nd of November. I'd like to greet the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and Madam Registrar who is back with us now after a long break. I would also like to greet everyone else present. We are starting 45 minutes late because of problems we had in bringing the accused here for reasons I am not familiar with. We'll try to make up the time lost. If there are no particular issues to be raised, we'll bring the witness into the courtroom. Could the usher please fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I'd first like to make sure that you're receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say that you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you can tell me your first and last names, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I name is Fikret Cuskic. I was born on the 29th of February, 1956, in Trnopolje, Prijedor municipality, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you currently employed and, if so, what is your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not employed. I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993 did you hold a position of any kind? Did you have a job? If so, what kind of job did you have? And if you were a member of the military, which unit were a member of and what rank did you have at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By profession I am an officer. In 1991, in September, I left the JNA, and afterwards I was an officer of the Croatian army. I was an officer in the Croatian army. And in 1992, in July, I was with a volunteer unit formed in the Republic of Croatia. And with that unit, I arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Bosnia and Herzegovina I was a brigade commander. That was in 1992 and 1993. Towards the end of 1993, I became the commander of the Bosanska Krajina operations group in addition to having the post of a regular commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a rank of any kind as an officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991 on the 20th of July, I fulfilled all the legal conditions to become a major in the JNA. And I was suggested for this rank by the command. I was suggested to be given this rank. But on the 16th of September, 1991, I never -- I left the JNA, so I never used that rank. In 1992 there were no ranks in the BH army, so that was only in December. I think it was on the 23rd of December, 1993, that I became a brigadier in the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified about the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, either before an international or a national court? Or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before an international court. And in Bosnia and Herzegovina I have testified before the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was called as a witness for the Prosecution in the Meqtauf [phoen] case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were called as a witness in the Meqtauf case. Was this during the trial or during the pre-trial phase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. I'd like to provide you with some information. But first of all, how would you like to be addressed, as mister or my general? What form of address would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mister, but I was a brigadier, that was the last rank I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You prefer to be called mister. You will first have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel. They will be examining you today and perhaps tomorrow. According to the schedule we have, you will be testifying for a two-day period. After Defence counsel has completed their examination-in-chief, the Prosecution to your right will also ask you questions. They will conduct their cross-examination. After that stage, Defence counsel may ask you additional questions. The three Judges sitting before you may ask you questions at any point in time, but as a rule the Judges prefer waiting for the parties to complete their examination -- cross-examination before asking you questions. If Judges ask the witness questions, the parties may ask additional questions after the Judges' questions. Usually Judges ask questions to clarify a witness's answers, either because the Judge believes that there are certain gaps that need to be filled. You will notice that the questions put to you by the Defence will be different from those put to you by the Prosecution or by the Judges. Try to provide concise answers and clear answers to the questions put to you. You may not be familiar with this but we don't have any written documents concerning your testimony, which is why your oral answers are so important. If you don't understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. I would also like to point out that as you have taken the solemn declaration you have said you will speak the truth and this means you should not give false testimony. False testimony constitutes an offence and it is an offence that is punishable. Secondly, you will have to answer the questions put to you by both parties, but when providing an answer if you think that your answer might contain information that could be used to prosecute you at a subsequent date, in such a case you can refuse to answer the question. But in such an exceptional case which never the less may occur, the Trial Chamber can compel you to answer the question. However, you are granted a form of immunity and your answer can't be used against you. So roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding today. But I would like to ask you something else. You have told us that you testified as a witness of the Prosecution in the Meqtauf case. When testifying in this case, were you granted any particular protective measures? Did you testify in public or did the Prosecution grant you protective measures of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, the Meqtauf trial hasn't started yet. It will be on the 16th of December. I gave a statement in the pre-investigative phase. That's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at the moment you -- you should know that I can ask for this issue concerning your testimony in the Meqtauf case to be deleted from the transcript, from the recording. If you would like such measures to be taken you can ask for these measures to be taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, I will now give the floor to Defence counsel who will add some more information to what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cuskic, may I address you as General since I'm used to addressing you in this way?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Presiding Judge has provided you with a lot of information about these proceedings, but I would like to ask you to pause after I put a question to you. Since we speak the same language, it is necessary for my question and your answer to be interpreted to enable everyone in the courtroom to follow you. This is why I would be grateful if you could make a brief pause after I have put my question to you. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were a professional officer. Could you please tell me something about your educational background. Which schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I completed the military secondary school in 1975 -- in 1979 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you tell us about the last position you had in the JNA and which duties do you have at the time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The last position -- the official position I had was in the Varazdin garrison in the 30 -- 32nd [as interpreted] Mechanised Brigade. I was a commander of a mechanised battalion in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us when you left the JNA. Could you please tell us why you left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The main reason -- to be frank, there were a number of reasons, but the main one was that I became convinced it was no longer the JNA, it was no longer a Yugoslav army. It had become something else. Given the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, this army sided with one people instead of remaining the army of all the peoples in Yugoslavia. This army became a Serbian army, and that's why I left it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, where did you go on that occasion, and did you join another army?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I remained in Varazdin. And as of the 1st of December, 1991, I became a member of the reserve forces of the Croatian army in the 1st Mechanised Brigade in Varazdin. And on the 10th of January, 1992, I signed a professional agreement and started performing the duties of the command of an armoured mechanised battalion which was responsible for training all the members of the tank corps in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the Croatian army, and why, and when did you leave the army?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this since the answer will be complex. I stayed in the Croatian army until the 31st of December, 1992, officially. But in mid-May the headquarters of the Croatian army authorised me to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in the territory of Croatia, I was able to organise volunteers. In June and July, I gathered volunteers from Western Europe, Bosnian citizens. I trained them in Klana, near Rijeka. I quit the unit. And then on the 8th of July I entered Bosnia and Hercegovina together with the unit. But officially, in legal terms, I was still a member of the Croatian army. I received a salary up until the new year between 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Bosnian volunteers, did you join the defence and where did you participate in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I formed the unit in accordance with an order from the supreme command staff in Sarajevo. Sefer Halilovic issued the order and that's how I reached Bosnia. I first went into action in the Gorazde/Igman area. Was to lift the blockade of Igman. This was in the second half of July, and I participated with the unit in the liberation of Trnovo in 1992, in August 1992. And afterwards, as ordered by Mr. Halilovic, I and the unit went to the Travnik sector. Since you are familiar with the situation concerning Prijedor, Banja Luka, and Bosanska Krajina. There were a lot of refugees in the area, and there was the 1st Krajina unit in Travnik, and we wanted to help our area, and this is why we have been provided with authorisation to relocate in the territory of the municipality of Travnik. 8

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Travnik and where did you find accommodation for yourself and your unit?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Travnik on the 21st of August. And I think the unit arrived there on the 25th of August. The municipal staff in Travnik provided me with the school in Han Bila as a temporary base. This was just a base. But we were involved in operations in the area between Karaula and Jajce. That was after the 5th of September we were engaged in combat operations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your superior commander at that time, General, or your superior command rather?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: My superior command was the sector staff in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please briefly explain to us what was the general and military situation in Travnik towards the end of August 1992 when you came there with your unit?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I would like to share with you some of my thoughts of the general situation in the territory of Travnik municipality. The situation bordered on chaos and it is a bit of an understatement when I say that. There were tens of thousands of refugees in Travnik, mostly Bosnians who had been expelled from their homes. They either stayed in Travnik, or Travnik was just a transit point for them. It was a humanitarian disaster. There was a lack of everything. It was very difficult to provide these people with any humanitarian aid because the area was completely blocked. Roads to Herzegovina were bad and overburdened. And the other territory was controlled by Serbs. That is why it was very difficult to feed people. As far as the military situation is concerned, it was very complicated. Jajce was still free and its defence was recruited from the territory of Travnik municipality. There was a pocket or a corridor, rather, which went through Turbe and Karaula, through a forest in Kruscica and Ledice [phoen] all the way up to Jajce. At a great risk, Jajce could be helped to a certain extent. When I say "risk," I mean that this corridor was not more than 2 or 300 metres wide at places. On the other hand, the military organisation at that time was in its initial stages. There were a number of various military structures co-existing in the same area. There were HVO units, there were HOS units, there were Territorial Defence units, and there were also some MOS units. Not many, however, there were some. In the areas of defence facing the Chetniks, the areas covered were very small and fragmented. The defence lines were very long and not conducive to successful defence. Let me share an example with you. For example, the front line around Jajce was about 136 kilometres long. And it was manned by the Territorial Defence by a unit which was the size and the strength of a detachment. I don't know about HVO units, but those were also very small and fragmented during that period of time. The most tragic thing and the saddest thing of all was that Territorial Defence units were not equipped. Only a very small percentage of men had infantry weapons. There were no communications means. There were no transport means that would serve for manoeuvres. The overall logistic situation was extremely difficult. And one more thing that I would like to mention which is very important was the issue of staff. I am referring to the quality of staff. The staff were not up to the situation. They were not in the position to conduct the operations that were taking place. I am particularly referring to the lower levels, company commanders, detachment commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in such a situation that you have just described for us very succinctly, but also very well, as a legitimate army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence should have mobilised all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tell me, what was the composition of your brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The composition of my brigade was very specific. During that period of time my brigade was composed almost exclusively of volunteers. I'm talking about the 7th Brigade of the BiH army. We had about 320 men all together who came from some 60 municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina but most predominantly from Bosanska Krajina. They had arrived from 13 different European countries. And together with me, they arrived in Bosnia. In our unit we also had some Croats who hailed from the territory of Bosanska Krajina. The percentage more or less reflected the composition and make-up of the population in the territory from which most of the members of my unit came.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since there was general mobilisation, when you arrived in Travnik could you notice that there was an equal response to the call-up by Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs, or rather was the situation different?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was mostly replenished from the ranks of Bosniaks. There were some members of the Territorial Defence who were educated, who were former officers, who joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For example, the late Major Mihajlo Petrovic who is -- who was a native of Serbia. However, he remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina and was the commander of the Vlasic detachment which was part of the Territorial Defence of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Croatian population? What units did they join?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: They mostly joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, during my examination-in-chief I would like to use some documents. I would kindly ask for this binder to be given to be witness. We have ample copies for the Trial Chamber, for the registry, and for our learned friends in the courtroom. I apologise. Let me just wait for the binders to be distributed across the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you've told us that there were other units from the territory of Krajina there mostly composed of persons who had been expelled from Krajina. What units were those?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: There was the 1st Krajina Battalion in the Travnik barracks. At the beginning of November, it was transformed into the 1st Krajina Brigade. Its core was established in Zagreb in May. It arrived in Travnik in June, and it was given the barracks as their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the documents under the title "The 17th Krajina Brigade," numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4. Tell me, please, do you know what these documents are about, what they are regarding?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: These are orders to establish the 1st Krajina Battalion. They were issued by the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The second document is the order regulating its combat use, and it says that it will be under the command of the sector staff in -- the regional staff in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the record I would like to say that these documents are number 0432, 0466, 0458, and 0493. General, you may proceed. These documents are documents testifying to the organisation and the use of those Krajina units that you found in Travnik, or when you arrived there. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 1st Krajina Battalion, and in November it became the 1st Krajina Brigade. There is also a document on the establishment and a document regulating the combat use of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, during that period of time did you participate in any combat operations? What problems did the defence of Travnik face when -- after Jajce fell?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I have already said that on the 6th of September, 1992, we had our first combat operations as the 7th Brigade of the BiH army. And this was between Karaula and Jajce. The next combat operation was on the 13th of October due to a very difficulty situation in Jajce on the order of the regional staff of the Territorial Defence. We were engaged. This was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. requested by Jajce. We were engaged in the defence of Jajce. I remember Commander Blazevic. He was the commander of the HVO in Jajce. He was engaged in combat. The situation in Jajce deteriorated by the day because the Army of Republika Srpska was engaged in a very well-planned combat operations with a view to taking Jajce. The fragmented forces of the Territorial Defence and the HVO could not put up any defence against those efforts. And in psychological sense, and in operational sense, this all had an impact on the defence of Travnik. A particular difficult situation was felt after the fall of Jajce. A total of 35.000 people all of a sudden poured into the territory of Travnik municipality. And the most difficult thing of all was the fact that when Jajce fell, to this very day the withdrawal of the HVO from Jajce remains a mystery. All of a sudden over night without any announcement, they withdrew so that the Territorial Defence forces remained. And there on they were left out in the cold and they were forced to retreat from Jajce. And this had a long-term impact on the future relationship between the former allies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your 7th unit become engaged in another important operation at the access or route to the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The regional staff commander ordered that the unit become fully engaged in the defence of Karaula. This is a big village before Turbe and Jajce. And I personally was appointed, or designated as the commander of the Karaula detachment. However, in spite of incredible efforts to try to defend that area, we failed. And Karaula fell on the 15th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Karaula, were there any organisational changes in the BH army? And if there were any such changes, what kind of changes took place?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: At the time there were many significant changes. They were very significant in terms of strategy. There was the decision on the formation of the 3rd Corps, encircled Banja Luka Corps, with its temporary base in Zenica and brigades were formed in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. So the defence forces became more substantial. And the conditions were created to develop all elements of the system of defence in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. And this would make it possible to have a better system of command and control. And it would be possible to use 3rd Corps units more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell me, at the time did you assume any duties? If so, what duties did you assume and how long did you perform the duties?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, after the fall of Jajce the situation in Travnik was chaotic, and this had an effect on the 7th and the 1st Krajina and on the refugees because morale was bad and men who were able-bodied would disappear. And in order to bring units up to strength, in order to strengthen the system of command and control and make units were efficient, a decision was taken to form Krajina Brigade. So on the 25th of November, 1992, the 17th Krajina Brigade with its headquarters in Travnik was formed. It was based in the Travnik barracks, and I became the commander of that brigade. I performed those duties until the 7th of April, 1994. But for the last six months, from the end of 1993, in addition to having those duties I was also the commander of the Bosanska Krajina operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, which other BH army units, as far as you know, were formed at the end of 1993 in Travnik, with a command post in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: In the town of Travnik itself, the 17th Krajina had a command post, the 312th local Travnik Brigade had a command post, and the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade also had a command post in Travnik. In the territory of the Travnik municipality there was a 306th Brigade and its command post was in Rudnik administration building in Han Bila. It wasn't in the town of Travnik itself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me as far as these newly formed units of the BH army are concerned, were they up to strength? What sort of officers did they have? What sort of equipment? What sort of weapons? Were any changes made or did the situation remain such as it was in the Territorial Defence as you just described it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: With the formation of the 3rd Corps command the conditions were created for solving the problems present in the Territorial Defence. So, for example, at my request as the brigade commander, the command of the 3rd Corps and some of the reserve forces were transferred from other units in order to become members of my units. So it was possible to move officers from one municipality to another, from one unit to another. Secondly, as far as the logistics of the BH army is concerned, the situation became better, it improved. So far the units had to rely on War Presidencies for logistics supplies. And on occasion, the War Presidencies would also command Territorial Defence units. This was no longer the case. So the chain of command, the system of control, became strengthened. The corps commander had authority, he had the right to command all the units within the 3rd Corps. So these positive changes were soon felt. The system of command and control became more efficient as well as combat readiness, as well as the logistics supplies, and chain of information, standards, et cetera, all improved. And in the territory there were elements that provided command and control. Discipline was better, there were many other elements. But I can't go into all the details, however everything improved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please slow down a bit because the interpreters are finding it a little difficult to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of these positive developments, General, could you tell us: If you compared today the situation of the BH army before the 3rd Corps was created, with the situation a year later in 1993, as an officer, could you say how much progress was made as far as creating an army in that area is concerned?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In spite of the fact that that was perhaps the most difficult period for the ABiH and especially for the 3rd Corps, it's my personal belief that during that period much progress was made as far as the construction and development of the ABiH is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you became brigade commander, the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade, could you tell us what your main combat and military tasks were. As a commander, what tasks did you have and what duties did you have to perform as a commander?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, my tasks were the tasks of a brigade commander and I was responsible for subordinate units, for subordinate units, for the correct use of subordinate units. And as far as engaging in combat is concerned, bear in mind the specific structure of the 17th Krajina Brigade, which was mainly composed of volunteers and refugees, so they didn't have their own local territorial area, we became a manoeuvre brigade within the 3rd Corps and we were engaged in all areas of the BH battlefield whenever the need arose. So we would take on such tasks, because in spite of our desire to get Bosanska Krajina back, we thought that the shortest way wasn't perhaps the best way to get Bosanska Krajina back. So we got involved in the deep blockade of Sarajevo and in helping other BH army units, and sometimes we got involved in helping units that weren't involved in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, please have a look at document 5. Have a look at item 1. The date on the document is the 10th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Which binder is it in? Which section?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's in the first section, 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Number 5?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution number is P403. Could you tell me what item 1 means? In item 1 the tasks of the commander of units in given areas are assigned. What sort of responsibilities -- what sort of military responsibilities does a commander in a given zone have?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the 3rd Corps commander. The purpose is to engage the units of the 3rd Corps in a planned manner. They are to make subordinate units and commanders responsible for ensuring that certain areas in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps are stable, certain areas where they faced the Chetniks. And they're responsible for taking measures for liberating given areas. As a brigade commander, I can plan the defence in that zone, I can plan future combat operations in order to liberate territory in the zone of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you have command and control over in that zone?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I commanded my own unit and perhaps another unit assigned to me. For example, it says the 17th Mountain Brigade with the 1st Sabotage Detachment. So I have control over these units. But according to the standards of the former JNA and according to the rules of combat that we followed, it was my responsibility to act within the zone and to develop cooperation with all the organs of power, with the police, with commercial enterprise, with the civilian protection. And it was also my responsibility to cooperate with my left and right neighbour. So as a unit commander in a given zone of responsibility, these were the responsibilities that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the BH army units ever take full control over the territory they were present in, or was the situation different? Who had power over that area?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, look, the ABiH was under the civilian command of the BH Presidency. And as soldiers we had been trained and we were loyal to the civilian command. So General Hadzihasanovic received an order from Sefer Halilovic and later from General Delic. And I received orders from General Alagic later on. But as to taking over power, well, we can't speak about that. The Civilian organs of power had power. But the power had been divided between the HVO and the SDA on the other side. It depended on the situation in certain municipalities. That's how the situation went.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the serious problems that the ABiH had to face, mostly legitimate defence forces in the country. So could you please have a look at document number 6 and could you tell me: Since your brigade is referred to and other brigades as well whether this document reflects some of the problems that commanders had to face, some of the problems they had to deal with in those very complicated situations. The document is Prosecution Exhibit P330.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a record from a briefing that we had, a briefing with brigade -- with the brigade and the district defence staff. I can't remember the subjects discussed at the briefing but it's an authentic document and it reflects the situation and most of the problems that we had to face in December 1992. And this is characteristic of the 17th as I have already said. It was composed of volunteers from Bosniaks who were from Western Europe, and of refugees from the territory of Bosanska Krajina. On the whole these were people who had lost everything and this was the only solution for them. In December 1992 in the 17th Krajina Brigade, most people had only completed six classes of primary school and I think that this shows how difficult the situation was. In terms of command and control in such units we had to make great efforts in order to ensure that everything functioned properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now go back to some of the problems that you mentioned and some of the problems you faced after the fall of Jajce when there were certain misunderstandings as a result of the way in which the HVO had behaved in the course of those fights. Tell me, after that event were there any excesses, were there any incidents, were there any clashes? Did the HVO attack any ABiH units at the time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, look, incidents or axes, well, there were such things even before. Because in such a territory if you have two armies which aren't under a single command, incidents are inevitable. I personally thought that a conflict would break out because throughout history this has been the case. I'll just tell you about what I myself experienced. Often I would go to Croatia to visit my family who had remained in Varazdin. My combatants would return from medical treatment from London, Slovenia, Croatia. They would return from a leave that they had spent with their family, and often they would be maltreated at HVO checkpoints. Their equipment would be seized, their food would be taken from them at checkpoints. And they would be -- or men would be imprisoned and beaten up. This was especially the case in the Tomislavgrad area. Combatants of mine would be stopped, beaten up, imprisoned for no reason. And it was their greatest satisfaction to fight -- to beat up combatants from my unit who were of Croatian nationality. For example, Toma Kunovski and Mirko Dandic. I think Jajce fell on 20th of October, and there were even more serious incidents. There was a conflict in Novi Travnik on the 25th or 26th of October. There was an attack on Prozor and Bosniaks were expelled from Prozor. Almost everything -- all Bosniak property in Prozor was burned. So the fall of Jajce only made the situation in Central Bosnia worse. Because, you know, there is Gornji and Donji Vakuf near Prozor. That was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO was your proclaimed ally in fighting the JNA and the Serbian forces. Did they jointly participate in combat operations especially when it came to the deep blocking of the capital Sarajevo? Did they participate in those combat activities together with you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The only cooperation in combat that we had with the HVO was in the territory of Jajce municipality. As we were billeted in the Travnik barracks when I learned about the defence of Travnik and I was engaged with part of my units in the territory of Bijeli Buc, which was in the territory of Turbe. I had a situation that 90 per cent of the lines facing the Chetniks were held by the BiH army. Almost everything except for one small area in Vlasic plateau where the HVO was truly on the front lines, all the rest of the lines in Travnik municipality were held by the Territorial Defence, later on the Travnik Brigade. The HVO already at that time had their own defence lines which were behind our backs from Ocena [phoen] towards Gradina and Turbe. What was the objective of that, I really don't know. There was no military justification for that. As for the de-blocking of the town of Sarajevo, the HVO did not want to participate in that, they didn't want to help us in any shape or form. I would even say that they aggravated the situation and I'm going to give you some examples. When my battalion was marching towards Sarajevo, we stopped at the Kaonik checkpoints and there we were ill-treated. The unit was 5 or 600 units strong and they pretended they needed some more approvals on top of all the things we had. I apologise, I'll try to slow down for the interpreters. I apologise. I didn't finish. And during combat activities my brigade was engaged by the Territorial Defence as staff, not only in order to de-block Sarajevo, but to help Sarajevo towards the end of December and later on for the next two or three months. And very often we thought that our successes would have been greater if the HVO were to allow us to go through the territory of Kokoska in the depth of the Chetnik territory. However, they never allowed us to do that. On the contrary, they would make our soldiers waste time and lose their lives in the territories that were mined on the contact zones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as we're talking about the relationship with the HVO, can you please look at documents numbered 1 to 8. These are DH36, DH35, new number 0459, 0490, 0596, 0609, 0645. For the record, I have just read out the numbers of the documents that I've asked the witness to have a look at. I'm going to ask you a few questions about these documents, General. General, these are HVO documents. Have you ever seen them before? My second question to you is: Did you feel in real life that the HVO behaved in the way described in these documents?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I have never seen these documents before. If I had seen them, I believe that my behaviour and my decisions and actions at the time would have been different. These two first documents from the strategic level, documents that originated from Boban and Roso showed that the proclamation of secession and the proclamation of war and the request for capitulation issued to all the forces that were not part of the HVO in the so -- in the so-called territory of Herceg-Bosna. For every normal member of the Territorial Defence which was subsequently the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this was unacceptable. As for document number P0409, I felt this on a number of occasions together with my units. I told you that we were naturally turned towards Croatia because a lot of us had lived there, a lot of us had been volunteers from Croatia. We arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina and all of a sudden we couldn't pass. We were robbed at checkpoints. For example, towards the end of October 1992, owing to my ID card of an officer of the Croatian army, I survived the ill-treatment near Mostar. In January 1993 I was ambushed in the area of Gostunj. A member of the HVO confiscated my Jeep and all the equipment and arms that were in the Jeep. And the -- we also had examples that the wounded that we sent for check-ups in Zenica were ill-treated at checkpoints and beaten to death. There are documents proving that. Mr. Blaskic received our protest regarding the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell me: Where was your unit engaged in January 1993 and what combat problems and combat situation did it -- did the 3rd Corps of the BiH army face at the time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: In -- I would say from the moment the corps was established on the 25th of November, 1992, up to mid-December of that year, we made a lot of effort, maximum effort, in order to train the command of our brigade. We tried to introduce order and discipline into the command and the subordinate units. We tried to improve the logistics in the brigade because the convoys and the aid that we had received so far from the countries of Western Europe were cut off at the time. We also tried to strengthen those elements of the brigade that supported the control and the command system in the brigade. I'm referring to the communications system. We tried to enforce the bodies for moral guidance and security. We tried to reinforce the military police and all of the logistics that existed in the brigade. Up until the end of December, we had two battalions completely ready to be used. Towards the end of December on the order of the corps commander, my battalions were sent to the zone of the 1st Corps and was -- were resubordinated to the command of Visoko in order to carry out some operations. Later on my 2rd Battalion was engaged and then the 3rd Battalion of the 7th in Krajina Brigade was engaged. In the subsequent period between the new year and the beginning of April, save for a very short period of the first combat with the HVO towards the end of January 1993, we were absolutely engaged in -- on the front line facing the Chetniks under Visoko frontline. I've already said in the introduction we were already considered to be the manoeuvre brigade of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened during the first conflict with the HVO in the territory of the 3rd Corps? Where was your brigade at the time or where were parts of your brigade at the time and how were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: At that time I had the 1st and the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Brigade. They were in Visoko. The 1st Battalion was undergoing establishment. We did not have enough weapons for three battalions, unfortunately. And this would be our combat deployment. In the general area, there were already fierce attacks on the part of the HVO, on Gornji Vakuf, and the situation in Gornji Vakuf became very critical which had an impact on the Lasva Valley and the central Bosnian area. After mid-January, ethnic cleansing started in the territory of Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade, did you receive certain tasks and missions to deploy your troops in some of these territories?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Based on the assessment by the 3rd Corps commander, my units were engaged as follows: The 2nd Battalion from Visoko was given the task to start moving via Prapratnica, Kocuni, Fornica, and to arrive from the Gornji Vakuf sector in order to help defence there. My 1st Battalion was given the task to March across the Lasva junction and Zenica to Han Bila and to be prepared for a possible HVO attack in that area. At the beginning, my support unit remained in Visoko. Later on there was another order by the 3rd Corps, according to which this unit was deployed in Janjici village in order to be ready to provide fire support to the units which were engaged on that axis. The 3rd Battalion was still under formation. It was in the barracks in Travnik. It was not ready to be used in combat because it didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you, General, to look at the part of the binder called Dusina. Can you please look at documents 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8. This is towards the end of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give us the numbers again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH47, DH45, DH46, DH48, P524, DH49, and DH50. You will find these numbers on top of these documents, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and the first document is: "Order: Administration for the military police." This is a document issued by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian defence council.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you been able to locate the area where these documents are found. Can you please look at these documents, all of these documents save for document number 5. At this moment I do not need you to look at this document because I want to ask you questions about the series of documents that I've just mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I've read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These are documents issued by the HVO and its bodies. Firstly, did you ever see these documents before? The situation as it was in January 1993, did it correspond the contents of these documents? The orders that you received at the time, did they have anything to do with this type of behaviour on the part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: My comment about these documents would be as follows: One can see that at the highest strategic level the H -- the BiH was being treated as an enemy force. Secondly, new terminology was being used. We were no longer the army. We were a Muslim element on the strength of the HVO. And one can see what the goal of all of this was, to disable the functioning of the BiH army in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina by blockades, by disarming them, by engaging in plunder, by resubordination, by incarcerating people, and so on and so forth. On the grounds we could feel that. Of course, if I tell you that at the exist from Zenica towards Ovnak, you know the structure of the population in Zenica and the ratio of forces in Zenica. The HVO had a checkpoint. They stopped people, and they acted according to these orders. In Kadnik a few kilometres from the Lasva junction on the road towards Kakanj and further on towards Vitez and Travnik they did the same. At the bend, the notorious bend near Travnik, at Miscema, on the forest road from Travnik to Novi Travnik, and now, it is only now that I understand why they behaved the way they did. On the other hand, instructions, positions, orders issued by the command and commander of the 3rd Corps were as follows: At any cost avoid conflicts and not get engaged in conflict. Respond only if there was a direct attack. I have to point out that I attended a meeting with the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, in Travnik in mid-October 1992. It was said at that time to the commanders and members of the territorial staff that a conflict with the HVO should be avoided at all costs. This is what Mr. Izetbegovic said. We suffered a lot. We tried to preserve our dignity, we tried to alleviate the situation, to avoid conflicts at all costs with certain officers with whom we could communicate, such as was Mr. Filipovic in Travnik. We tried to deal with the situation together with him, however the situation deteriorated and now I understand that there were orders to that effect from the highest levels of command of their forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as you were explaining where your units were deployed pursuant to the orders of the 3rd Corps, you mentioned that the HVO occupied a territory some 2 or 3 kilometres from the Lasva junction. Can you tell me: As an officer, what was the importance of that junction and what is the responsibility of a corps commander in order to secure such a position or such a feature.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The Lasva junction is the biggest communication hub in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. There is a railroad there going from Visoko to Zenica, there is a crossroad of roads leading from Vitez to Zenica and from Travnik to Zenica, a Travnik/Kakanj/Sarajevo road as well. And a military responsibility with regard to that junction required from any commander to take measures in order to secure such a feature. Because this place was very important from the military and strategic point. On the other hand, the situation that prevailed on the grounds, requested from all the bodies, the customs, and all the other bodies that functioned at the time, very few of them that they did in order to control the territory to prevent smuggling, illegal moving of people, goods, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you've told us that you received certain combat missions and tasks at the time. Tell me, please, did you receive an order to send a mortar battery and to deploy it in that area?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I did, but at another stage. The order to move the battalion -- well, I think it was after the 20th of January that I received that order. In order to take up a firing position and to be ready to provide artillery support, this is an order I received a few days later. A firing position was taken in the village of Janjici, but this battery wasn't used because it arrived later on, and infantry action had come to an end. Some sort after a cease-fire had been arranged. So fire wasn't opened from that position, from those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I said that the charges claim that units of the 17th Krajina were involved in attack on Dusina, what would your response be? Did your units participate in any way in the combat around Dusina or in the attack on Dusina?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Not a single unit, not a single member of the 17th Krajina was in a position to participate in the fighting in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at document number 5, Prosecution Number P129, and tell me: Is this order that you have just described and is this a battery that was never used for the purposes stated in this order.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: That's the order and that's the battery concerned. It mentions the firing positions and the battery's tasks, but as I said the battery was not put into use. I can also remember that I informed the corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, after conversation he had with Mr. Izetbegovic in Geneva. Well, there was propaganda on the Croatian television as to which we had burned down Croatian monasteries, we had massacred the Croatian population. But I know that on the 26th an order was issued to halt all activities and not to fire a single bullet. And this is an order that I as a soldier respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the events that you described in the attacks of the HVO on Prozor, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Vakuf, tell me: At the time as a brigade commander did you feel that there was a plan that the HVO had to take control of the territory?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, I had my own belief. I had assessed the situation and I thought that the HVO strategy was to try and take the area town by town. They managed to do this in Prozor but not in Travnik. In January they managed to do this in Busovaca. In April, they managed to do this with Vitez. In June they tried to do this in Travnik, but they were stopped there, more or less. So their strategy was to pursue the Vance-Owen Plan that hadn't been accepted or signed. And naturally this couldn't be accepted without policies having been adopted. This couldn't be done by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, when did you return to Travnik with your unit?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I returned to Travnik with my unit at the beginning of April, I think it was on the 7th or 8th of April, I know it was just before Easter and tension was escalating, tension between the HVO and the army was rising. This resulted -- this was the result of Dario Kordic's visit to Travnik. Dario Kordic said that Travnik would be a Croatian area and said that units had to be disarmed and resubordinated, et cetera, et cetera, and this was a factor that increased the tension in the town. When arriving in Travnik I felt that the situation was very tense. You could smell this in the air. We were expecting something ugly to happen, and the subsequent events just confirmed this. On the other hand, I apologise, in military terms the HVO had already occupied all the elevated positions around Travnik from the Vilenica relay and then Sipovik, from Sipovik to St. Antoni chapel, they had directed pots and pans [as interpreted] on Travnik. And about 50 kilometres from my barracks they had already become entrenched in a hill there and would go into action at night. In the barracks, 18 of my men were wounded, although war had not been declared.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that unfortunate incidents occurred. What happened in April and what sort of an effect did this have on the members of the ABiH, or rather what sort of additional tasks did army commanders have to carry out to avoid a full-scale conflict with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said in relation to the town tension was high. They said that Travnik would be the capital of Herceg-Bosna. The tension was great and the HVO had deployed its forces in a way that showed that they wanted to take full control of the town of Travnik. And on the 16th of April, we had the events in Ahmici. And this wasn't just a spark, this was a fire which brought the situation which was already very bad to a head. The barracks at the time -- the barracks that are still in Travnik now, it's across the road from the Travnik hospital. My combatants would observe the wounded being brought there from Ahmici. My entire command was engaged in action, made efforts to ensure the system of command and control functioned properly. And we managed to prevent soldiers from engaging in a conflict with the Croats. And I think that other commanders in the peripheral areas in the Vitez municipality, commanders of the 306th and perhaps commanders from Busovaca and Zenica, I think these commanders found it far more difficult to control their units and to prevent them from carrying out chaotic attacks and taking revenge, et cetera. And similarly in towns some Mafia and criminal circles intended to take indiscriminate revenge against the population in Travnik. But by issue orders, by engaging units, et cetera, we managed to prevent such issues from occurring.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in May did the situation improve? Were relations improved? And what was done to deal with that difficult situation that the army had to face? Were any decisions taken that you thought would enable you to avoid a full-scale conflict with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, look, our side made great efforts to avoid a conflict. The commanders did everything they could. There were frequent meetings with the political leadership of the War Presidency and of the HVO as well. Attempts were made to find a compromise and to avoid a conflict. In Travnik a joint command was formed and HVO officers and 3rd Corps officers from the Travnik area became part of this command. Their objective was to avoid a conflict. An operations plan was drafted which provided for many measures that should be taken. It drafted a plan for action against our joint enemy. And I thought that this conflict would be avoided. We had already started preparing to liberate the territory of Bosnia and Krajina and to face the Chetniks. So my sabotage detachment was given a task to go to the Vlasic and Jajce axis. And my reconnaissance men went to Jajce and returned from that area. Some of the combat units, I'm referring to the 3rd Battalion, was engaged in the area of Bijela Budje, in the area facing the Chetniks. We hoped that this operations plan made -- the level of the joint command would be implemented. We hoped we would really start fighting our common enemy together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it is a good time to have a break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now have a 20- or 25-minute break and we'll resume at about 5 to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that you were hoping that the joint command would create the conditions for you to engage in fighting together. Did the HVO accept such cooperation in the month of May and what was the situation like at that time in the area of your brigade and the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, look, while the brigade commander of the HVO in Travnik was Filipovic, they would officially state that they wanted this operations plan to be implemented. And when Leotar became the head of the HVO brigade in Travnik, he's from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and just before the conflict he became the brigade commander of the HVO in Travnik. And there were individuals from the brigade command, above all people from the village. For example, Gaso and Lovrinovic. There were indications that it would be implemented, but they were only paying lip service to this. There were still checkpoints, HVO checkpoints, on the roads, the main positions around the town were in the hands. And in the course of the night they would open fire from those positions on the town of Travnik. Many civilians in Travnik were wounded and I have already said that there were members of my unit in the barracks were wounded. This was reported by the local and foreign media. CNN and BBC reported on these events. And this shows that the situation in Travnik was one that the world was familiar with, because at the time propaganda and Croatian television was terrible. The way they portrayed the Bosniaks -- well, they were portrayed in a way that showed them in a criminal light. I won't go into all of this, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the documents under the heading "Relations with the HVO." Have a look at the following documents: 9, 10, and 11, and tell me whether these documents reflect the situation such as it was in May 1993. 9 -- the documents are 0999 and then 1087 and the final one is 1096.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: These documents are a partial reflection of the situation. This is perhaps just the top of the iceberg. It reflects the incidents that the HVO were involved in, the acts committed against our citizens and citizens of Travnik. You can see that there were men who were brutally beaten. Members of my unit, and I still have this image before we, this image of bruised and wounded men. In the second document, there are a number of such examples and this is an accurate reflection of the way in which the HVO behaved just before the conflict broke out between the 20th and 30th of May. And the last document is a protest from Commander Alagic. It relates to an incident. And unfortunately I was a victim in that incident. It took place on the greatest Muslim holiday. We went to a Bosniak village because a celebration had been planned there by members of our unit, an ambush had been lain for us. And they shot in between my legs and above my head. We were humiliated, insulted, they stole our things from us. So if they are ready to do this to a commander of an operations group, to a brigade commander, well how do you think they behaved towards ordinary privates or towards the citizens of Travnik who weren't regular members?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in such a situation can the fact that the town was surrounded, that the HVO soldiers had taken up position on elevated positions around the town, tell me what happened in June. Was the town of Travnik attacked at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that the factors mentioned already only made the situation more complicated. Members of the 312th were killed. There was the massacre in the village of Ahmici. Bosniaks were expelled from the territory of Vitez municipality. Wounded men were brought in in May. The HVO acted in provocative ways, opened fire, wounded men. So this was all concentrated in this area. So as to whether the HVO thought that Bosniaks would start fleeing from that area, as to whether they thought they could take control of the situation I don't know. But on the 3rd of June Travnik was attacked, there was an all-out attack. The artillery was used, multiple rocket launchers were used, and the HVO had fully surrounded Travnik and had linked up the Croatian settlements to the south-west with Doca [phoen] and the territory of Novi Travnik and Vitez. These villages had been linked up. We had to return fire and embark on an operation to remove the threat. That was the result of the attack from Slimena on Travnik. So there was a frontal conflict with the HVO in the territory, in the entire territory of the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, at the time were you confronted with the fact that the HVO was no longer alone in attacking the ABiH? At the time were they cooperating with the Republika Srpska army when implementing their plans?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of the conflict -- it's not at the beginning of the conflict that we came across this factor. In May we received information according to which the HVO had played a match with Chetnik forces, and they went to Banja Luka afterwards and drank there together. In Galica on the 13th of May, 1992, the Serbian forces killed 13 HVO soldiers. Furthermore, there were intercepted conversations in the military district of Vitez. And in the area of the command of the 22nd of the Republika Srpska army on Vlasic. There was information on agreements that they tried to reach in the case of conflict between the army and the HVO. We were counting on cooperation between the Republika Srpska army and the HVO. We were expecting such cooperation. This is what actually happened. It's a historical fact that the HVO completely evacuated the population, its forces, from that area, because they couldn't occupy Slimena. And on the Vlasic plateau they tried to move the troops to Vares. And I think on the other hand an agreement had been reached to take positions of the Republika Srpska army that were held by the HVO at the time. That was Veliki Kik in our zone and the area of Vlasic facing the relay transmitter. We managed to prevent this. On the other hand a few days later I think in mid-June, on the 14th of June, the Republika Srpska army in the area of Novi Travnik managed to come from the flank and take our line on Bijeli Buc. And by engaging all the forces that we had, we managed to regain the line and prevent a break-through of the Chetnik forces because according to the documents we later captured, a commander from the 19th brigade, we found out that they had planned to break through to Miscema and Vilenica. This would have resulted in the loss of Turbe for us and Travnik would have been surrounded by Chetnik forces, and Travnik would have been in a very difficult situation. They would have -- probably have been able to take the Bratstvo factory of arms and this is something that could be seen from the documents that had been captured from the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, under the HVO and Republika Srpska army, can you look at documents from 1 to 5 and can you tell me, please, whether these documents reflect the situation that you have just described for us. Do these documents describe the relationship between the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska? For the record while you're looking at the document, these documents are DH232 ID, DH233 ID, and documents D1130, D1129, and D1140.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The first document is the document that I see for the first time; it is very interesting. The command of the 1st Krajina Corps issued an order to the command of the operations group on Mount Vlasic to support the HVO with artillery fire. Item 2 of the said order shows that it had provided for the medical care of HVO soldiers who were wounded. And the document points to not only cooperation but the co-action on behalf of the two allies who had one common enemy which was us. The second order, or the second document regulates more precisely how the artillery support would be provided in order to avoid fire being opened on UNPROFOR. This served to prevent the Republika Srpska army to come under fire on the part of the UNPROFOR forces. The third document, which has 12 items and I'm going to focus on two key ones -- actually, I'm going to focus on the introduction which shows the objective of this order. It says here that representatives of the HVO requested from us to take positions and then when the civilian population is left they surrendered. And later on the document regulates the way how HVO soldiers would be treated. It is obvious that BiH army in the Travnik sector could have found themselves in dire straits if this had been implemented. Owing to our combat readiness, good command and control, and the intelligence we had gathered, this did not happen, thank God.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you tell us something about document number 5. You have already mentioned what happened with the civilians in the territory.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me I would like to go back to document number 4 and comment upon it. The HVO had a good chain of command and good propaganda. It forcibly evacuated their own population from Travnik and some 30 families from Bilic [phoen]. The propaganda said that the Krajina men are coming, they will torch and burn your village. And in the 7th and 9, the Chetnik lorries collected all the weapons and the civilians were evacuated to the Galica plateau. The propaganda up there was so powerful and so strong. I can tell you that my family resided in Varazdin at the time. In conversation with my own wife, when I spoke to her, she asked me: Is it possible that this is what you are doing down there? And my own wife, with whom I had two children at the time, had to be told by me: Woman, how could you believe that I could torch a church or something like that. On the other hand, Mr. Ranjinga [phoen], deputy commander of the Travnik Brigade, showed an order to me to allow evacuation of all Croatian civilians from Travnik. At that time Commander Alagic was not accessible to me. I didn't allow that because it was not our goal to perform ethnic cleansing. Our goal was to eliminate the military threat which would possibly result in us being eliminated from the territory, from this area. And document number 5 is a document issued by the president of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. represent, Dr. Radovan Karadzic ordering the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army to escort HVO soldiers with their weapons through the territory of Republika Srpska all the way to Vares. They were not to be captured, they were not to be retained. They were to be transported to Vares. And the Croatian civilians were to be escorted either to Hercegovina or to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can you please tell me whether during those combat activities when you were defending Travnik, did you capture some of the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: As far as my brigade is concerned we did have prisoners of war from the ranks of the HVO. And their number differed depending on the development of combat activities. We had anything between 40 and 20 prisoners. We interviewed all these men, and if we realised that they were at home during combat operations, we would let them go home without weapons. We kept the weapons because, as I already told you, I had an entire battle without any weapons. On the other hand, members of the HVO for whom there were some indications that they had committed war crimes or similar crimes, the competent bodies took over those cases and their numbers ranged between 10 and 20. It depended largely on the period of time and the overall development of the situation. It depended on whether criminal reports were issued and whether they were transferred to Zenica and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell me: Where were these prisoners of war accommodated?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Members of the HVO were in the prison in the Travnik barracks. This was a very typical facility that used to belong to the former JNA. On the upper floors there was one battalion of my brigade. And in the basement there was a prison. And one part of the communications centre and one part of the unit for the anti-electronic combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before these people were imprisoned and accommodated there, who was accommodated in that prison? Who was kept in that prison?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: When the 3rd Corps was established and their -- and its brigades, we took a lot of measures to introduce order and discipline into our ranks. And in order to establish our army within those activities, I had to institute the disciplinary measures against a number of my soldiers who had committed all sorts of violences. So they would be kept in the prison until criminal reports were issued against them and until they were transferred into the hands of the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what were the conditions like in that prison which your brigade had in the barracks. What were the conditions for the members of the HVO who had been incarcerated there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The prisoners of war which we had in the 17th Brigade had the same conditions as my soldiers had if they were remanded in custody as disciplinary measure. Their accommodation was the same, their food was the same. They were engaged in some work. There was no distinction being made between members of my unit who had committed certain offenses and our prisoners of war. At the initial stages, until the moment I received full instruction from the command of the 3rd Corps as to how prisoners of war were to be treated, I tasked my assistant commander for morale as to how these prisoners should be treated. Together with a priest, Pavo Nikolic, who were the most senior Catholic priest in Travnik, they would have weekly religious service, they would have three to five cigarettes a day as well as my soldiers, they had three meals a day, they were allowed to celebrate their religious holidays. This is what we were able to provide for them and this was in accordance with standards and international conventions. We had cooperation with the International Red Cross, and the bodies of the 3rd Corps also controlled conditions of our prisoners and they always commended us for the conditions that we provided for them in the prison in the barracks in Travnik, the barracks in the 17th Brigade was billeted in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did anyone at any period of time when prisoners of war were incarcerated in the prison of your brigade ever have any objections about the bad treatment of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever had any objections. Representatives of the Red Cross, Father Pavo Nikolic, the families of these prisoners of war all commended us. They had a lot of trust in the way we treated them. I still bump into some of these people in Travnik and they buy me drinks because I had treated them correctly while they were imprisoned. I believe that we provided these people with the conditions that could be provided for under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at the part of the binders containing documents about the incidents in June. Can you look at document number 2 bearing the Defence number 1189. This is a document issued by the Croatian Defence Council, the security services. And at that moment when this document was issued, they were your enemy. Can you please look at the document and once you have looked at it, can you pay attention to page 2 of the B/C/S text. The first paragraph speaking about the delegate of the International Red Cross. Even your then-enemy, did they accept that the conditions that were offered to the incarcerated members of the HVO were the conditions that met the standards and provided for the appropriate treatment of the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is clear from this report. It says here that the conditions were satisfactory and that the number of prisoners of war was not great. I would like to repeat that members of the HVO from Slimena and Dolac who were at home and who were disarmed at home, a few days we released. And that is why there were only eight persons in the military prison. At first this number was higher. There was some 40 of them at the beginning of the conflict. As soon as we linked up with the Slimena and as soon as my security organ established what the situation really was, they were released and they were sent home to their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the criminal charges were brought against some of these individuals. At the moment when this was done, did the military commander have any responsibility towards such individuals?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: No. The commander's responsibility stops there and the competent body are -- bodies of the judiciary which are not part of the military. So the military responsibility stops when the criminal charges are instituted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, General, what happens if a person against whom criminal charges have been raised and who is transferred to the judiciary bodies and if such a person is supposed to be exchanged for one reason or another, what happens then? Would a commander or the BiH army as such have any role to play in that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: According to the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina that prevailed at the time, there was a procedure established involving such persons. There were such persons against criminal charges were instituted for even war crimes. And such persons were exchanged. There should -- there should be the institute of abolition that preceded the exchange, and only after that these persons could be exchanged for other persons kept by the enemy army. And this was done with the mediation of the international institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to move on and ask you what was the relationship of the BiH army and especially your brigade and you as their commander towards the protection of cultural and religious facilities. A little while ago you have mentioned propaganda and the conversation that you had with your wife. Now I would like you to tell how you implemented protection on the ground. What was your attitude and the attitude of your soldiers towards such facilities and toward such buildings?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, all the regulations, all the instructions issued by your superior command, all the guidelines, all the orders, provided that civilians and should be protected as well as religious buildings and the cultural heritage. In the zone of responsibility of the Bosanska Krajina operations group. If there was such buildings in the operations zone, so to speak, the military police would provide security for them. If these buildings were in an urban centre where there was no combat, the MUP would provide security for them. Or if the clergy thought that such buildings could be under threat, we also provided security by using the military police. So such buildings were always protected, either by the military police in the zone of operations or by the civilian police in areas where there was no combat. But on the whole this was our responsibility and this was something that we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your attitude towards religious facilities in Travnik and towards members of the clergy who had remained in the town after the fighting on the 3rd and 4th of June?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I personally believe that we had a correct attitude, military and civilised attitude, towards religious buildings in the town of Travnik and towards members of the clergy. I personally -- I was personally present when Cardinal Puljic visited Travnik in mid-June - I can't remember the exact date - and he expressed a satisfaction with the attitude of -- the ABiH's attitude towards religious buildings and members of the clergy who had remained in the territory which was under UN control [as interpreted].
