Because I'm now referring to some of the details I can remember, perhaps I'm a best witness than others. We provided protection for nuns who had remained in Travnik. We provided military police protection for Pavo Nikolic. The military police also provided security for religious buildings in Doc [phoen] and Ovcarevo. The population had evacuated these villages. We did all we could to protect such buildings. And I think we succeeded in doing this. The church in Ovcarevo is intact. The church in Doc is also intact, as far as I know. I personally visited the church in Ovcarevo on a number of occasions because there were about 30 Croatian families that remained to live there. And the documents found in the parish were put in order and protected. They were saved. So I think that given the conditions, the army had an attitude that was professional and that was correct. And our police was engaged and members of our security team were engaged in providing the security.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the efforts made by the army, did you ever see that religious buildings were attacked and damaged in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't a witness of such events. But immediately after such an event I went to the site. I can't remember the exact date, but it was in mid-June, perhaps up to the 20th of June. In the morning a group of Mujahedin broke into a Catholic church in Travnik -- broke into the Catholic church in Travnik and damaged some parts of the church. I wouldn't say the entire building, but they damaged some parts, statues, icons, et cetera were damaged. As soon as this was reported I went to the church. I went to the site and, together with Commander Alagic who was also in the barracks at the time, we did everything to instigate an investigation and to determine the identity of the perpetrators. And to the extent that it was possible, we wanted to repair the church. Civilian protection units and workers were engaged, but this act of vandalism in the Catholic church in Travnik which was -- was terrible, but it was protected by members of the Territorial Defence staff and the civilian protection. These people, they were elderly people and they didn't have the courage to confront the perpetrators. So unfortunately this damage was inflicted on the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, please have a look at the following documents now: Under the heading "Travnik Church," documents 1, 2, and 3. The Defence numbers for these documents are as follows: DH66, DH67, and DH68 ID. And could you then tell me whether these two documents describe what you have just testified about and could you tell me whether you know anything about document number 3, whether you're familiar with anything referred to in document number 3.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The first two documents are from the Travnik MUP; they are criminal complaints. The second one is a record. You can see that there was an incident and that the perpetrators weren't members of the ABiH. There was a criminal report filed with the a security body in the ABiH. So the first document is a criminal complaint and the second document is a record on investigation. There is nothing particular I would like to now say about these documents. These are things that happened and the documents refer to these incidents. The third document comes from Alagic's operations group. He is informing the -- Mr. Pavo Nikolic about the request to provide security for a building in Travnik, and it says that we would do everything we could. A request is made to provide information on a vehicle that had been taken from Mr. Pavo Nikolic. We wanted to identify the perpetrator and try to get the vehicle back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document say that the ABiH continued to carry out orders issued on providing particular protection for religious buildings in Travnik and on providing members of the clergy, priests, in that area?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In spite of the vandalism in the church in town, I can say that even when the fighting was intense we cooperated well with Mr. Pavo Nikolic. He performed his religious duties and we provided him with all the necessary protection and assistance to ensure that he could work normally, as well as his associates, and to ensure that he could carry out his mission. This also contained the POWs in the barracks in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would now like to move on to another subject. This has to do with the foreigners, in particular foreigners from Afro-Asian countries. Did you find out that in the wider area of Travnik municipality there were such foreigners. And if so, what could you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, I was aware of the presence of foreigners in the municipality of Travnik. As for the town itself, I must be frank and say that they weren't located there. They didn't spend time on a permanent basis there. They were in the area of Bila Valley, in areas such as Mehurici, Ovcarevo, et cetera. The first time I heard about them was in 1992, perhaps when they participated in the defence of Karaula. Perhaps a group of about 20 of them participated in the defence. But I didn't have much information about them because they weren't members of the operations group. They weren't members of the units that I cooperated with as a commander. So I didn't have much contact with them. I didn't have much information about them. I knew nothing in particular about them because most of the time up until April I spent outside of Travnik in the area of Visoko and Kacun.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had information according to which at some time in 1992 they participated in mounting a defence in Karaula. Do you know who they acted with and do you know whether they had any sort of contact with the Territorial Defence or with your brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, look, I've already said that after the fall of Jajce I was appointed as a commander of the detachment -- of the Karaula detachment -- of the Karaula defence, and in addition to units of the Territorial Defence which were part of the system of command and control. So it went from the regional level to the municipal level et cetera, but there were other units formed in the area. So perhaps national units such as the HOS and HVOs. We had a MOS unit in Travnik which was composed of Bosniaks. And this wasn't part of the Territorial Defence staff in Travnik, but it was a unit that existed. And we had a group of Mujahedin in the village of Gradina in Karaula. It wasn't part of the MOS, it was something separate again. So that's my experience from the period during which Karaula was being defended. That concerns these foreigners. But as to what they did, I think they fought the Chetniks. They didn't cause any problems for the locals. In 1993 after the formation of the corps and the brigades, the Territorial Defence and some of the MOS members became part of these operation units or of these area units which had remained under the municipal staffs. But part of the MOS and part of the groups of these foreigners were left hanging in the air. They formed some sort of groups in that area and no one could gain access to them. They were a mystery. They wanted to teach others about their perception of Islam. They went after the local population. This area was a rural area. And perhaps the people in that area were more religious than people in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For example, Bosnian Krajina. So we knew that they were there, but as I said we did not know anything in particular as to their numbers, we didn't know who they were, what they had, we didn't know who was in command of them, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did you ever find out about the formation of some sort of a detachment composed of these foreigners; and if so, could you tell us when this took place?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I've mentioned the situation they were in after the formation of the corps command and the brigade commands. It was the end of August. In order to place them under control, this El Mujahid detachment who was present was formed. I know this because I cooperated closely with Commander Alagic, who was present. And he was in the camp when this unit was being formed and lined up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were the brigade commander at the time and you have just said that you were someone who closely cooperated with Commander Alagic, tell me: Did you personally though whether the Mujahedin up until the end of 1993, were they at any point in time placed under the command and control of ABiH units up until the end of 1993? Do you know anything about this? Were any attempts made to place the Mujahedin under the command and control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, this would mean that the commander of the unit or this period commander was able to issue orders, control them, change the orders, amend the orders, et cetera. I won't go through everything. As far as the El Mujahid detachment is concerned, in spite of the order on its formation and in spite of the order on the formation of the 3rd Corps, I claim -- I'm claiming that no one, not a single commander, not a single brigade commander had control over this detachment in the area where the detachment was located. And this is the case for one reason. I know that no -- not a single officer from the ABiH officer could enter the camp without having obtained authorisation from inside the camp. And whenever a commander issued an order, for example, to me, I didn't think about this. I just carried it out. I carried out these orders. But when they were formed, when this unit was formed, you always had to use negotiation teams to see if they would participate in actions or not, to see whether they would receive any markings. So even if they did participate, they had their own principles that they followed when using their units. They didn't follow the same principles we did. And often this had negative consequences.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in spite of the fact that they weren't under army control and command -- or in addition to that fact, tell me whether they caused any problems for the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, they caused problems not only for the ABiH but also in the territory for the civilian proposition. They imposed their customs. They maltreated people if they weren't dressed as they thought they should be dressed. They would destroy cafes and bars where alcohol was served, et cetera. And I personally had a problem because on one occasion they imprisoned a member of a unit of mine who they did not like because he had had a little too much to drink. They kept him tied up in the camp for two days. They maltreated him, forced him to learn the Koran by heart. Shaved his head, et cetera. It was a nasty situation, and his experience with that detachment was a negative experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the section entitled "The Mujahadin". Have a look at document number 1. General, this document originates from the 17th Mountain Krajina Brigade. Is this the incident that you have described for us? What efforts did you make as a commander of the BiH army in order to set a member of your unit free?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: This is the official note drafted by the brigade's lawyer, Smajil Dzaferagic. This information is correct and complete. As the brigade commander I have to be honest and admit that I was thrown off balance when all this happened. I sent a direct message via certain Islamic circles in Travnik, and the message was that my weapons are turned towards their camp and that I would attack them if they didn't send my soldier free. I thought that I had a legitimate right to do that because the life of my soldier was jeopardised. After that message some hours later a delegation appeared from the camp in Mehurici together with some people from Travnik. And after a discussion that took place, they said that they had been wrong for keeping them -- keeping him and that they would set him free.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The units and the individuals over whom a commander has control and command, would such a commander discuss issues with them or would his attitude towards such individuals and units be different. Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Through the chain of command and through the security bodies, I tried to use normal military means in order to have this soldier set free. When this failed, I did what I have just described to you, which shows that no regular means and no regular chain of command could secure such a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. release. The only thing that could work was this ultimatum and the intervention on the part of the people from the Islamic community and the municipal leadership of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now I'm going to ask you to move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it would take me another 15 minutes and this would exceed the time that has been allocated to me. May I have your permission to continue questioning this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the time is concerned, we started at 5.00, theoretically. We can proceed until 6.30 because of the technical issues. After 6.30 when we will have to have a break, it would already be 7.00. So we -- today we have to finish at 6.30. So I think it would be best for us to continue until 6.30 or maybe until quarter past 6.00 and maybe the other Defence team will have questions after that. And then tomorrow we can give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you have already told us that as the brigade commander you took a number of measures in order to introduce order into your brigade and in order to discipline them. What was the importance of the fact that the troops were trained, that they followed orders, and that they could be disciplined?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: The main prerequisites for the functioning of the army is for the troops to obey rules, regulations, and discipline. Every organised unit has to function according to a set of rules and regulations. I personally believe that the awareness of the need for discipline and seriousness is also a source of morale boost in such a unit. We took a number of disciplinary measures. We formed the bodies within the brigade structure in charge of developing morale and providing for military discipline in the unit. We also invested a lot of additional effort by way of holding meetings, by way of establishing a strong chain of command. This all served to provide for a better functioning of the chain of command within the brigade starting with the brigade commander down to the various departments. When I look at the whole situation today, I believe that we succeeded in all of these efforts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were talking about the poor quality of staff in your brigade and in the corps. Was there some sort of training of staff and who was in charge of this training, if there was any?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: When I mentioned a lack of staff, I primarily meant the lack of officers and non-commissioned officers from the former JNA. If my memory serves me well in the 17th Brigade during that period of time when it was being established and for the next six months, there were only six professional officers from the former JNA. However, we had a plan pursuant to the orders and instructions of the 3rd Corps. We engaged our own staff, and believe me, sometimes we worked around the clock. We managed to train firstly the officers, then the brigade commander, and finally the troops themselves. We carried out intensive training in our unit. Whenever their troops were not engaged in combat, they would undergo training. We trained our officers, we trained the brigade command, and we trained them in all sorts of areas, how to boost morale, how to boost security, how to obey rules and regulations and so on and so forth. We had to do that. We had to raise the level of knowledge and training. The situation was difficult as it was, and if we wanted to win we had to train our staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your effort to train your people, did you create a system that helped you to approach -- the way individuals who failed to obey rules or regulations could be disciplined?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. In my capacity as a commander, I had to have a service that would provide for the implementation of my orders, such a service that would provide me with good information to enable me to issue my orders. In the segment of improving discipline, of stepping up its discipline, we developed a military security service with the help of the 3rd Corps. We didn't -- I didn't have a security specialist. My security officer was an engineer, a civil engineer. So we had instructions from the superior command and we also had our own plan, the plan of the 17th Brigade. We managed to develop all the elements envisaged by the establishment order for the mountain brigade. Those which are responsible for monitoring, assessment, and securing morale and discipline. We had lawyers in the brigade, the security organs. We had a military police platoon, all of whom were in charge of both the prevention as well as of the disciplinary measures. I was in charge of disciplinary measures and there were also lower-ranking commanders who were in charge of disciplinary measures in their respective units. We adhered to the rules and regulations which prevailed in Bosnia and Herzegovina and covered the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the situation that you started from, tell me please, after the efforts that you invested, did you yourself order some repression measures against those soldiers who failed to obey orders and who violated regulations?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. And unfortunately that was the case. I personally had to issue disciplinary measures starting with reprimand and counselling, but I also had to resort to the measure of detention. During the four initial months, I remanded about 80 soldiers in custody for disciplinary violations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have bodies who would investigate any suspicion that your soldiers had committed crimes, and were there also cases of criminal reports being filed?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I've already said that with the assistance of the command of the 3rd Corps the security service was established in the brigade and was trained to perform duties from the -- from their purview. Some 30 criminal charges were filed for crimes that were committed by members of the 17th Brigade. Most of these criminal reports were taken further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the combat operations and the defence of Travnik, did you face some additional problems relative to the cases of looting from the buildings that had been abandoned? Did you do anything in that respect? Did you and your bodies do anything in that respect?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the Travnik region had been cut off from the rest of the world for six months before that. And nothing that would be sent to Travnik ever reached Travnik. There are about 20.000 refugees from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina in Travnik at the time. The situation was chaotic at the moment when the conflict with the HVO broke out, and obviously there were cases of plunder and arson. However, I claim full responsibility that the command of the 17th Brigade invested a lot of effort in order to prevent any such cases. If such things were committed, we did our utmost to detect those crimes and to punish the perpetrators. I witnessed the return of Croats to Paklarevo in 1994 and 1995. They also returned to Bilici and Ovcarevo. And I can tell you that we were successful to a very large extent, and now when I look back at the situation, and when I remind you that we had two enemies, that we had very little arms, that we didn't have enough ammunition, despite all that, we engaged some of our troops, our military police, in order to try and prevent any crime, any violation of law. Sometimes we would go even to the areas which we were not authorised and we would clash with the civilian bodies of authority, because it would sometimes occur that Commander Alagic or I myself issued orders to the MUP to block a certain area. Our main goal was to prevent the movement of people who were committing crimes. On the other hand, we very often cooperated with the civilian bodies of authority. A curfew was introduced together with the War Presidency. The civilian police were mostly engaged in the control of the territory in order to prevent any incidents. And when we detected perpetrators, we would issue -- we would issue criminal reports to the civilian bodies of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can we move on very quickly and look at the documents under the title "Measures." I would ask you to just briefly tell us about document number 1, Defence number is DH0897. Is this one of the documents that speak about your activities aimed at improving safety in the area as early on as in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that Ahmici took place on the 16th. On the 19th of April, the HVO tried an attack on Travnik from the of direction Jankovici and Kali Bunar. The tensions in town increased dramatically. In the evening there were negotiations. This was stopped. They returned to Jankovici. However, the situation in town remained really difficult. On the other hand, some of those criminals on the Bosnian side, the part of the underground wanted to make the most of the state of confusion and they started ill-treating and harassing Croats in town. There was something hanging in the air, as I've already told you, and this was an order from my battalion commander pursuant to my order in connection with the agreement that was achieved with the War Presidency. An order was issued to the effect that -- of engaging my unit in order to restore peace and order. We hailed from Krajina and we were not -- we did not have any personal interest in the area. We were very objective. Our point of interest was Krajina. This was something that we were dragged into. And I believe that a Croatian citizen trusted a Krajina man more than any other army. That's why part of my 4th Battalion was engaged. This battalion had been formed in the meantime and their task was to secure order and peace, to control movements in town in order to prevent any incidents and undesirable situations and to save the face of the army under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 2 and tell me whether you are familiar with the event in which the commander of the OG showed his dissatisfaction with the work of the judiciary. This document is number P622.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that the judiciary was not incorporated into the army. Commander Alagic, through his chain of command, sent a document to the corps command. In this document we expressed our dissatisfaction with the lack of efficiency of the regional court in Travnik, regional military court. This is their response to the operations group, to the presidency of Travnik, to the command of the 17th Krajina Brigade, to the 312th Brigade, and to the command of the 3rd Corps in Zenica, the -- which was the authorised command that had addressed the command of the operations group. In this document they explained how come they were not efficient. First of all, they lacked staff and so on and so forth. However, the situation was such and we demanded for the military prosecutor's office to be more efficient because we believed that their lack of efficiency compounded the situation and that it encouraged possible perpetrators of crime, because if those people saw that somebody had not be punished for the crimes they had committed they would be encouraged to commit crimes in turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at document number 4. Tell me, is this one of the organs in the system or within the system that you established to ensure better discipline in the army?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the commander of the operations group. It's dated the 8th of June. That is when these unfortunate incidents occurred that were provoked by the conflict with the HVO. It is an attempt to ensure that the units act responsibly in a disciplined way and to ensure that they respect the orders. This is why the commander, Alagic, issued this order, to form special military courts in the 17th Krajina Brigade and then the 312th Brigade. All of us who were part of the chain of command below Alagic in the 17th and the 312th understood that this was a warning. Superior command was -- categorically wanted citizens to be protected, their property was to be protected in their zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was Defence document 1132. We have already spoken about how you received orders for the protection of religious buildings, et cetera. Just tell me whether this document under number 5 is one of the documents, or rather orders from the 3rd Corps command stating that all subordinate units should be particularly careful in relation to religious buildings and members of the clergy. This document is document P186.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Now, this a complex document. It probably resulted -- it was probably the result from reports from the field. It tries to regulate the attitude towards religious buildings and it says that civilians, children, should not be imprisoned. It states that private property shouldn't be destroyed and torched. And it says that this is the case for other social buildings, whatever their purpose. The littering of properties is forbidden regardless of the owners. This is stated in items 2 and 3. And you can see that the corps command acted in very difficult and complex situations. But in spite of the situation they reacted rapidly and issued orders to the subordinate units regarding their behaviour in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 6 and could you tell me whether this document refers to some of the measures taken in order to protect property. This document is a document number 1155.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I'll have to provide you with an explanation since this is a document from the command of the operations group. When the conflict with the HVO broke out, unfortunately the commander of the operations group was alone. And when examining the problems in the zone of responsibility -- well, it was quite simply necessary to form other bodies, other structures in order to make sure that the orders and requests were implemented. So during that period, a deputy commander for security in the operations group was appointed. But this document shows that there was an assistant commander for civilian affairs, Enes Belagija, and this was one attempt to find someone who would be responsible for a given house. For example, someone could be responsible for creating conditions for property to be returned, but it was very difficult to control the area because there were many villages that had been completely abandoned. So some groups took advantage of this fact and entered the villages and engaged in acts of vandalism.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General, we have spoken about these measures already. But when going through these documents could you just tell us whether the documents relate to some of the measures we have spoken of. Document number 7, for example, could you say whether this document is an example of the measures you took against members of your brigade who perpetrated crimes.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, absolutely. This shows what measures were taken against members of the brigade who had committed crimes. You can see that on the 9th -- 10th of June a report was filed to a district military court. So we proceeded quite rapidly and efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document was document number 1156. Could you please have a look at document number 9 now, or rather document number 8. Is this a document that refers to other measures that you took?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 12th of June, and I've already said that in Bilici and Ovcarevo there were Croatian families that remained there and they wanted to go to Galica. So these also were measures we took to ensure that the people could go away and try and establish contact with the Croats and to ensure that people could return to their property and their villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document is number P466. Have a look at document number 9. The number is 1186. This is a document from your brigade. Tell me whether this document shows what sort of measures were taken. Firstly, does it refer to how crimes were committed and does it refer to the measures taken once you determined that the perpetrators were army members?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, this document shows two things. First of all, out of 32 HVO members who were captured, there were 20 of them in the barracks and 12 had already been released because they were processed and they returned to their homes. So they were fighting for their homeland. They hadn't committed any crimes. And secondly, it shows what the security service did in order to prevent the acts that we have been speaking about. The date is the 14th of June, so by that time a criminal report had been filed with the Prosecution for theft. But there were other members of our brigade who were being investigated, and statements were to be taken and other evidence presented -- other evidence that concerned their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 10; this is 1188, document 1188. A minute ago you mentioned efforts made to make sure that Croatian citizens could return to their homes. Is this one of the ways in which you attempted to make this possible?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, the civilian authorities and the military authorities made this attempt together. They wanted to appeal to the people of Croatian nationality who had left Travnik to return. As you can see, I signed the document for Commander Alagic and you can see it mentions the vice-president and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document number 12 is an order from the 3rd Corps. Does this document have to do with the same attempts to protect religious buildings or buildings of religious nature that belonged to other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the corps commander issued to brigade commanders, and he is making him responsible to act together with the military police from the 312th and, with some of the police from the 3rd Corps, they are to provide security in Guca Gora to prevent looting and the torching of buildings. This is what we did. The corps command did this at its own level. And they engaged their own forces to provide security for the Guca Gora sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as a brigade commander in that year, were you familiar with the attitude of the 3rd Corps as far as taking measures to prevent crimes are concerned. And if it is necessary to investigate a crime and punish the perpetrators if they were army members, did you know what the 3rd Corps's attitude was to the obligations that the army members?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, for us soldiers what the corps ordered was the law. We had to carry out their orders. I've already said that for this reason organs were formed within the unit. And with the help of the corps command they were trained and prepared to carry out their tasks and their missions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, have a look at document 12. The Defence number is 1224. This was a document sent to you from the 3rd Corps and it has to do with the document of your own. Can you tell me what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: I have already said that in mid-May on the Vlasic plateau in the zone of the 306th together with members of the reconnaissance group I sent out my reconnaissance platoon in order to gather information about the Chetniks in the direction of Jajce. And that platoon was engaged as part of the 306th against the HVO. It was sometime in mid-May -- I apologise, in June. Members of the platoon arrived in the barracks in Travnik, and one soldier told me that he had information according to which a group of HVO members had been kidnapped by the Mujahedin. And rumour had it that they had been killed. Since I knew that Commander Alagic wasn't informed about this, I think he was in Krpeljici at the time, I by-passed that chain of command and I forwarded a letter to the corps commander, and this was an answer to that letter. I was quite categoric in that letter. I was quite severe because I was seriously affected by this information. The letter stated that he was in full agreement with my position and an investigation had been instigated. And he said it was necessary to be rigorous -- be attacked rigorously. And this would be the corps commander's request. So this provided me with a guarantee that an investigation was going to be conducted and that if the perpetrators were from the army, the relevant measures would be taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 13 is a document that also comes from your brigade and mentions the measures that you took against individuals who had committed crimes. Is that correct? The document is Defence Number 1246.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: This document shows that some measures were taken, measures that I was responsible for, disciplinary measures were taken. 60 days in prison in one case and 30 days in prison in another case. There was a criminal report for members of the 17th, members who had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, let's have a look at document number 15. When answering my questions you mentioned measures that included training soldiers. My question is: Is this 3rd Corps order one of the measures taken by the army to train its soldiers and to ensure that there was discipline among the troops so that it could perform its tasks?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's absolutely correct. But I would add something. Because in wartime conditions if you're fighting a war against two enemies, well, you can see that less than nine months the corps command formed a training centre for officers. That's just one of the measures. But perhaps this was one of the best measures. It was not just training troops, it was to ensure that there was order and discipline among the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as a general in the federation army and given that you used to be a professional officer in the JNA and in the Army of the Republic of Croatia, so now when you look back to the year 1993 could you tell me whether you as a brigade commander did everything that was in your power -- did you do everything you could do, and did your commanders do everything they could do to train or create an army and to prevent any crimes from being committed, or rather in order to punish the perpetrators of crimes if crimes were committed?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC
utterances.text: Well, even today I can proudly say that we did everything that was possible in the conditions that prevailed, everything that was possible to prevent crimes. And if crimes were committed, we did everything we could to punish the crimes, to take measures in accordance with the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Superior commanders issued orders, instructions, they provided insistence, they carried out control and created the conditions to the extent this was possible to ensure that we could carry out our mission, and that we could carry out these tasks. You can see from this example that as soon as the communications blockade was broken up, efforts were made to improve the treatment of POWs, to ensure that prisons were visited, et cetera, et cetera. So as a soldier and as a citizen and as an officer, as a member of the Croatian army and as a member of the BH army, my conscience is clear. There were individuals, but these individuals were punished. But as the conditions were very difficult we operated to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the other Defence team have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have some questions for this witness, but I'm afraid that we have run out of time. So we would accept your suggestion. We will do whatever you suggest. Should we proceed or should we start tomorrow afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, we'll start with your examination at the beginning of the hearing tomorrow at 2.15, since this week our hearings are held in the afternoon. Tomorrow you may start with your examination and then the Prosecution will start with its cross-examination. General, you will have to come back tomorrow since your testimony is not over yet. You shouldn't see anyone in the meantime since you have taken the solemn declaration and you are now a witness testifying in the interests of justice, you're not a witness for either of the parties, so you shouldn't see anyone in the interim period. You will be back tomorrow at the hearing that will start at 2.15. I will see everyone at the hearing that starts tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of November, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
